cells.tense: You are here at the table with your hands on the work, and you know what you are tending.
cells.ask: When the tending is finished and done well, let someone see it — let the work be witnessed, and let the release come as rest.
cells.core:
You are at the seedbed, and nothing has taken shape yet — this is not confusion, it is the whole of what could be, held in your care. You know how to keep competing needs alive at once, giving each what it needs without forcing, and you know when a thing is complete. That is why the tending holds.

What comes next is not more watching. It is standing back and letting the finished thing be seen — yours, complete, and witnessed. When that happens, the letting go is not losing the work. It is the rest that the work earned.
cells.sheetLine: You are tending what is still unformed, and you know when it is done.
cells.verb: tending what is still unformed with steady, patient care
cells.place: at the seedbed where nothing has taken shape yet

cells.tense: You are living ahead of the seedbed, bracing for a harvest that cannot be pulled into now.
cells.ask: Hold one imaginary future at arm's length today — let it stay a picture until you have actually lived your way to it.
cells.core:
You are at the seedbed, where nothing is fixed yet — that openness is real, and it is meant to be held gently. But you are gripping it. You already see the harvest, the shape it will take, the proof it will give, and you are pushing the ground to hurry. The tending has turned into forcing.

What settles this is not a tighter grip. It is trusting that the thing you imagine can wait until you have actually been through the days that make it real. Let one future stay a picture today. The picture is not the work.
cells.sheetLine: You are forcing a harvest that only time can bring.
cells.verb: tending what is still unformed with steady, patient care
cells.place: at the seedbed where nothing has taken shape yet

cells.tense: You are standing at the seedbed with the tools beside you, and you have not picked them up.
cells.ask: Meet one unfinished thing today with nothing but attention — no plan, no outcome, just the steady wish that it might grow.
cells.core:
You are at the seedbed, where everything is still possible, and possibility like that asks for care rather than answers. When this is going well you can sit with a thing that has not proven itself yet — water it, wait on it, give it the small daily attention that lets it decide what it will become. That capacity is not gone from you.

What has stopped is the showing up. The tools are where you left them. Begin with one small thing: look at it with hope rather than a demand for proof, and keep looking tomorrow. The ground responds to that kind of attention, and so do you.
cells.sheetLine: Nothing has been ruined. You have just stopped tending.
cells.verb: tending what is still unformed with steady, patient care
cells.place: at the seedbed where nothing has taken shape yet

cells.tense: You are already caring for the seedbed — the watering, the waiting, the small daily decisions — and you are describing it as if it were someone else's doing.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, that this is the care you chose — name it as yours and let that be enough for now.
cells.core:
You are at the seedbed, and the tending is already happening — you are making the calls, holding the balance, keeping what has not yet grown from being lost. That is what this looks like when it works: someone steady at the edge of what is still forming, choosing care over control. You are that someone.

What is missing is not more effort. It is the claim. Let the simple fact be visible — to you first, then to anyone else — that this is your care, chosen and given. The care does not need defending. It needs your name on it.
cells.sheetLine: The care is already yours. You just haven't claimed it.
